newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S&P assigns new ratings to 13 Indonesian banks.
newsitem.headline: S&P assigns new ratings to 13 Indonesian banks.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp said on Monday it has assigned public information ratings to 13 Indonesian banks.
The new ratings employ analytical procedures that parallel traditional credit ratings, but differ in that they are based on public disclosure and other sources of information, S&P said.
The following banks have been rated:
S&P said that to meet future competitive threats from overseas institutions, Indonesian banks need to become stronger, faster and fewer in number.
"Standard and Poor's regards the existing 240 commercial banks as far too many for the Indonesian banking sector at this stage of the country's economic development," S&P said.

"The system has too many banks but not enough branches relative to other financial systems. A bank that is too small is unable to take advantage of economies of scale in information technology, funding and human resources training," it said.
S&P said it is not confident that the small- to medium-sized Indonesian banks can compete with fellow Association of South East Asian Nations banks when barriers to entry fall.

But it said the 1995 shift in market share dominance to private sector banks from government or state-owned institutions signalled an important trend towards heightened professionalism in Indonesian banking.

Likely government support, if needed, is a major factor leading to generally higher ratings among government-owned banks. But, over the medium term, S&P said the outlook for large private sector banks is more favourable than for many of the state banks.
As the privatisation trend continues, government support of state-owned banks may change over time, S&P said.
